result: DAS is a deep-learning method for annotating acoustic signals that uses temporal convolutional networks (TCNs) with optional integrated preprocessing to produce hierarchical representations of sound features. The method outputs confidence scores for each song type at each audio sample, which are then converted to annotation labels through thresholding and post-processing.
evaluation: Claims C4, C48-C61 describe the architecture and working principle of DAS, supported by detailed methodological descriptions and Figure 1. The use of TCNs with dilated convolutions (C53-C57) and optional preprocessing (C48-C52) are well-documented design features. The output format and post-processing steps (C58-C61) are clearly described with supporting figures.

result: DAS accurately annotates Drosophila melanogaster courtship song from single-channel recordings, achieving 97% precision and 96% recall for pulse song and 92% precision and 98% recall for sine song, outperforming the existing FlySongSegmenter (FSS) method particularly for weak signals and high-frequency pulses.
evaluation: Claims C72-C85 present quantitative performance metrics supported by experimental data in Figure 1D-M and Table 1. The comparison to FSS (C71, C73-C74) and human annotators (C82) is well-documented. Performance improvements are attributed to context exploitation (C80-C81) with supporting evidence in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C. Temporal precision measurements (C83-C84) are appropriately quantified.

result: DAS successfully processes multi-channel audio from nine microphones for fly song annotation, achieving performance comparable to FSS (pulse: 98% precision/94% recall; sine: 97% precision/93% recall) with high temporal precision.
evaluation: Claims C87-C92 are supported by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3. The multi-channel processing approach (C88) is described, and performance metrics (C90-C92) are quantified and compared to FSS. The use of separate networks for pulse and sine (C89) is documented in Table 2.

result: DAS accurately annotates mouse ultrasonic vocalizations (USVs) with 98% precision and 99% recall, demonstrating robustness to noise (90% recall at SNR 1/16) and generalization across sexes without retraining.
evaluation: Claims C100-C107 are supported by experimental data in Figure 2. Performance metrics (C100-C102) are quantified and compared to specialized methods (C103, Table 3). Cross-sex generalization (C104-C106) is demonstrated in Figure 2H. The experimental setup (C95) and signal characteristics (C96-C97) are clearly described.

result: DAS achieves high performance on noisy and variable marmoset vocalizations (96% precision, 92% recall, 4.4 ms temporal error) when trained on only 1/9th of the data used by a previous method, while providing millisecond-resolution annotations compared to 50 ms resolution of the prior method.
evaluation: Claims C111-C113 are supported by experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1. The comparison to prior work (C110) provides context, and the improved performance with less training data and higher temporal resolution (C112-C113) is well-documented in Table 2.

result: DAS accurately annotates Bengalese finch song with 97% sample-wise precision and recall, 0.3 ms temporal error, 98.5% correct syllable type classification, and 0.012 sequence error, performing as well as specialized deep-learning methods.
evaluation: Claims C120-C124 are supported by experimental data in Figure 3 and Table 2. The experimental setup (C118-C119) is clearly described. Performance metrics are comprehensive and well-quantified, including temporal precision (C121), syllable classification accuracy (C122), and sequence error (C123). Comparison to specialized methods (C124) is documented in Table 2.

result: DAS robustly annotates Zebra finch song with excellent precision and recall despite increased syllable variability and background noise, demonstrating robustness to song variability and recording noise.
evaluation: Claims C128-C129 are supported by experimental data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2. The experimental setup (C125) and challenging conditions (C126-C127) are described. The inference about robustness (C129) is appropriately drawn from the performance data.

result: DAS is a universal method for annotating acoustic signals across diverse species (flies, mice, marmosets, birds) that performs as well as or better than species-specific specialized methods.
evaluation: Claims C130-C131 and C178-C181 are summary statements supported by the comprehensive experimental data across all species tested (Figures 1-3, Tables 2-3). The generality claim (C181) is appropriately inferred from the consistent high performance across diverse signal types and recording conditions.

result: DAS achieves high throughput (8-82x realtime on CPU, 24-267x on GPU) and low latency (7-15 ms), making it 3-10x faster than existing methods and suitable for both large-scale annotation and real-time closed-loop applications.
evaluation: Claims C134-C145 are supported by speed benchmarks in Figure 4A-B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1-2. Throughput and latency measurements (C134, C138) are quantified across species. Comparisons to existing methods (C141, Table 2) are documented. Explanations for speed advantages (C142-C144) are reasonable inferences based on architectural design. The suitability for applications (C140, C146) is appropriately inferred from the performance data.

result: DAS requires small to moderate amounts of manual annotation to achieve high performance (fewer than 50 annotations for flies and mice, 48 for zebra finches, median 8 per syllable type for Bengalese finches), with training completing in less than 10 minutes for 90% performance and under 5 hours for full training.
evaluation: Claims C149-C161 are supported by experimental data in Figure 4C-E and Figure 4—figure supplement 3-4. Data requirements (C149-C156) are quantified for each species. Training times (C158-C160) are documented. The iterative training protocol (C148) is described with supporting figures. The identification of an annotation error (C154) demonstrates quality control.

result: DAS can be combined with unsupervised methods to facilitate annotation work, successfully recovering known syllable types in flies, marmosets, and birds, and revealing annotation errors in manual labels.
evaluation: Claims C170-C175 are supported by experimental data in Figure 5 and Figure 4—figure supplement 3. The unsupervised classification successfully recovers syllable types across species with varying degrees of success (marmosets show more variability, C172; zebra finches show one-to-one mapping, C173). The detection of annotation errors (C175) is documented in Figure 4—figure supplement 3C-F. The approach is well-motivated (C164-C165) and appropriately described.

result: DAS can be optimized for new species without expert knowledge using a user-friendly interface, with network performance being robust to changes in structural parameters, making automatic annotation widely accessible.
evaluation: Claims C182-C184 are supported by experimental data in Figure 4C-E and Figure 4—figure supplement 5. The robustness analysis (C183) demonstrates that performance is maintained across a range of parameter values. The inference about accessibility (C186) is appropriately drawn from the combination of ease of use, robustness, and availability of pre-trained networks (C185).

result: Acoustic communication is widespread in animals and studying it requires accurate, fast, and robust annotation methods, but existing methods face challenges with weak signals, speed, and adaptability, creating a need for a general annotation framework.
evaluation: Claims C1-C29 establish the motivation and context for DAS. These are primarily background claims supported by citations to prior literature (C10-C27) and logical inferences about requirements (C2-C3, C22-C28). The gap in existing methods (C28) is appropriately identified based on the cited limitations.

result: Deep neural networks are powerful tools for annotation tasks, but existing spectrogram-based approaches for animal vocalizations have limitations including unsuitability for some signal types, need for manual tuning, and slow recurrent units.
evaluation: Claims C30-C32 and C40-C47 provide background on deep learning approaches and their limitations. These are supported by citations to prior work and represent established knowledge about the field. The identified limitations (C44-C47) motivate the design choices in DAS.

result: DAS provides a graphical user interface for annotation and training, can be trained with little manual annotation, can be combined with unsupervised methods, and produces annotations with low latency suitable for real-time applications.
evaluation: These claims (C6-C9, C35-C37) are summary statements about DAS capabilities that are supported by the detailed results presented elsewhere. They serve as overview claims that are substantiated by the specific experimental results in other claim groups.

result: Future improvements to DAS could include self-supervised learning to reduce data requirements, extension to handle overlapping signals from multiple animals, and integration with pose tracking for context-specific optogenetic manipulations.
evaluation: Claims C187-C192 are speculative statements about future work. While the suggestions are reasonable and supported by citations to relevant methods (C187-C188, C192), they represent planned or potential developments rather than demonstrated results. The limitation regarding overlapping signals (C189) is acknowledged but not experimentally validated.
